name: NVIDIA HGX platform as sold inside OEM and system-builder servers
vendor: NVIDIA (HGX board/baseboard) via Supermicro, Dell, HPE, GIGABYTE, QCT, Wiwynn, Inventec, Foxconn
region: Worldwide; manufacturing concentrated in Taiwan and ODMs (NVIDIA states Vera Rubin is ramping into full production with Taiwan's top server makers and global supply chain leaders)
notes: QUOTE-ONLY. The HGX platform page itself funnels buyers to a marketplace 'Explore Systems' link rather than to any price, so no figure is recorded. The genuinely useful fact here is the BASIS: HGX is a baseboard+GPU platform, so when you buy 'an HGX system' the accelerators come WITH the system and are not separable line items. NVIDIA notes HGX Rubin NVL8 integrates eight Rubin GPUs on sixth-generation NVLink, can be paired with NVIDIA Vera CPUs (HGX Vera Rubin NVL8) or with x86 CPU baseboards. Practical sourcing consequence: there is no such thing as ordering one H100 SXM or B200 module from an OEM; the minimum purchase unit is a 4- or 8-GPU node, which is exactly why per-GPU numbers quoted against this channel are 5-10x higher than bare-card prices elsewhere. Lead-time rather than in-stock is the realistic status for new-generation HGX; no week count is published so lead_time_weeks is null. EXPORT CONTROLLED (true). Regime: US BIS advanced-computing export controls (the Oct 2023 interim final rule, 88 FR 73458 - source sup-buy-bis-2023-advanced-computing-controls), which put datacenter accelerators under ECCN 3A090/4A090, added the advanced-computing Foreign Direct Product (FDP) rule, and extended Regional Stability (RS) controls to Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5. For items destined to Macau or Country Group D:5 the rule applies a PRESUMPTION OF DENIAL; other RS destinations get a presumption of approval. Practical effect: which accelerator you can legally be sold, and which SKU counts as compliant, is set by destination and end user - not by the channel.
